questions.stem:
In this question you must show all stages of your working.
Solutions relying on calculator technology are not acceptable.
$$\mathrm{f}(x) = 4x^3 - 8x^2 + 5x + a$$
where $a$ is a constant.
Given that $(2x-3)$ is a factor of $\mathrm{f}(x)$,

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) use the factor theorem to show that $a = -3$
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Substitutes $x=\frac{3}{2}$ into the expression, sets equal to 0 (may be implied for this mark) and rearranges to find $a$. Condone invisible brackets for this mark only and condone arithmetic slips in their working. Substituting $x=-\frac{3}{2}$ is M0 and attempts via long division score M0.
A1*: $a=-3$ achieved with no errors seen including the omission of brackets. There must be sight of $x=\frac{3}{2}$ which may be embedded in the expression or $\mathrm{f}(\frac{3}{2})$ followed by at least one intermediate stage of working/manipulation (it may just be the left hand side of the equation), before proceeding to the given answer. The "=0" must be seen somewhere in their working before the given answer.
Official notes (completeness pass):
- $(\mathrm{f}(\frac{3}{2})=)\ 4(\frac{3}{2})^3-8(\frac{3}{2})^2+5(\frac{3}{2})+a=0\Rightarrow a=...$ M1; $\Rightarrow\frac{27}{2}-18+\frac{15}{2}+a=0\Rightarrow a=-3$ * A1*
- e.g. $4(\frac{3}{2})^3-8(\frac{3}{2})^2+5(\frac{3}{2})+a=0\Rightarrow a=-3$ is M1A0; $\mathrm{f}(\frac{3}{2})=\frac{27}{2}-18+\frac{15}{2}+a=0\Rightarrow a=-3$ is M1A1. Note the trivial case $\mathrm{f}(\frac{3}{2})=3+a=0\Rightarrow a=-3$ is M1A0 (not enough shown)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Hence show that the equation $\mathrm{f}(x) = 0$ has only one real root.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
Work done in (a) must be made use of in (b) to gain credit.
M1: Attempts to find a quadratic factor of $4x^3-8x^2+5x-3$ using $2x-3$ as a factor: score for $2x^2\pm x\pm...$ if algebraic division is used or score for $2x^2\pm...x\pm1$ if equating coefficients/inspection used. Alternatively, they may attempt to find a quadratic factor using $x-\frac{3}{2}$ as a factor so score for $4x^2\pm2x\pm...$ if algebraic division is used or score for $4x^2\pm...x\pm2$ if equating coefficients/inspection used.
A1: $2x^2-x+1$ (for $2x-3$ as the linear factor) or $4x^2-2x+2$ (for $x-\frac{3}{2}$ as the linear factor)
dM1: Attempts to show their quadratic factor has no real roots. It is dependent on the previous method mark. Factorisation attempts are M0. Accept via an attempt at $b^2-4ac$ for their quadratic factor so score for values correctly embedded in $b^2-4ac$ for their quadratic; an attempt to solve their $2x^2-x+1$ or $4x^2-2x+2$ using the quadratic formula with values embedded or via a calculator (you must check their roots are correct for their quadratic); an attempt to complete the square e.g. $2(x\pm\frac{1}{4})^2\pm...$
A1*: Requires correct factorisation of the cubic, correct calculation for the quadratic, reason and conclusion. For example, after factorising their cubic to e.g. $(2x-3)(2x^2-x+1)$ (which does not need to be explicitly stated) accept e.g. the discriminant of $2x^2-x+1$ is $-7<0$ so only has a root at $x=\frac{3}{2}$. If correct values are embedded which give $-7$ then this is fine. (For $4x^2-2x+2$ the discriminant is $-28$); or $2x^2-x+1=0 \Rightarrow x=\frac{1}{4}\pm i\frac{\sqrt{7}}{4}$, $(2x-3)=0\Rightarrow x=\frac{3}{2}$ so only one real root. (The roots will be the same for $4x^2-2x+2=0$); or $2x^2-x+1=0\Rightarrow 2(x-\frac{1}{4})^2+\frac{7}{8}>0$, hence $x=\frac{3}{2}$ is the only one real root (The completed square form for $4x^2-2x+2$ could be the same or a multiple of it depending on how they have rearranged their inequality). There must be some reference to the root $x=\frac{3}{2}$ either by stating it or indicating the linear term has a root (e.g. writing "root from here" next to it), but do not accept incorrect statements such as only real root is $(2x-3)$. Condone "solution" for "root". Do not allow statements such as "Math error" without interpretation of what this means.

questions.stem:
A circle $C$ has centre $(2, 5)$
Given that the point $P(8, -3)$ lies on $C$

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) (i) find the radius of $C$
(ii) find an equation for $C$
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
Mark (i) and (ii) together.
(i) M1: Attempts to find the radius. Score for the values embedded in the expression e.g. $\sqrt{(8-2)^2+(-3-5)^2}$ or $\sqrt{(2-8)^2+(5+3)^2}$. They must be attempting to find the difference in the x coordinates and the difference in the y coordinates.
A1: $(r=)10$ ignore any units $\pm10$ is A0 Do not accept $\sqrt{100}$ for this mark. isw once a correct answer is seen.
(ii) Note that if M0 is scored in (a)(i) then this is A0 in (ii)
A1ft: $(x-2)^2+(y-5)^2="100"$ o.e. e.g. $(x-2)^2+(y-5)^2="10^2"$ or $x^2+y^2-4x-10y="71"$ Follow through on their positive single value of $r$. isw once a correct equation is seen.
Official notes (completeness pass):
- (i) $r=\sqrt{(8-2)^2+(-3-5)^2}=10$ M1A1; (ii) $(x-2)^2+(y-5)^2=100$ A1ft

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Find the equation of the tangent to $C$ at $P$ giving your answer in the form $ax + by + c = 0$ where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are integers to be found.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
B1: Gradient between centre and P is $-\frac{4}{3}$ (may be implied by their gradient of the tangent)
M1: Attempts to find the negative reciprocal for their gradient. May be embedded within their equation of the tangent.
M1: Attempts to find the equation of the tangent at P using a changed gradient (cannot just be a stated gradient of the tangent which is incorrect and does not follow from any earlier work) and $(8,-3)$. Score for $y+3="\frac{3}{4}"(x-8)$. The coordinates $(8,-3)$ must be correctly placed. If they use $y=mx+c$ they must proceed as far as $c=...$
A1: $3x-4y-36=0$ o.e. (provided all the coefficients are integers and all terms are on one side of the equation) isw once a correct equation is seen.
Alt (b) Alternative method using differentiation:
B1: $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{4-2x}{2y-10}$ o.e. such as $2(x-2)+2(y-5)\frac{dy}{dx}=0$ or e.g. $y=(100-(x-2)^2)^{\frac{1}{2}} \Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=-(x-2)(100-(x-2)^2)^{-\frac{1}{2}}$ (may be implied by $\frac{3}{4}$)
M1: Attempts to find the gradient of the tangent at P using their $\frac{dy}{dx}$ and the given coordinate(s). Do not be concerned with poorly differentiated equations for this mark and just look for the x (and possibly y) coordinate(s) to be substituted into a differential equation leading to a value for the gradient. Condone sign slips substituting in.

A1: As above in main scheme notes

M1: Sets equal to their radius: $(x-2)(x_1-2)+(y-5)(y_1-5)="100"$
M1: Uses the point P and sets equal to their radius: $(x-2)(8-2)+(y-5)(-3-5)...="100"$

questions.stem:
The binomial expansion, in ascending powers of $x$, of
$$(3+px)^5$$
where $p$ is a constant, can be written in the form
$$A + Bx + Cx^2 + Dx^3 ...$$
where $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ are constants.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find the value of $A$
(1)
parts.mark_scheme: B1: $3^5$ or 243 seen. Do not award if it is outside the bracket as $3^5(1+\frac{px}{3})^5$, but allow if some of the terms of the binomial expansion are found and 243 is the constant term. e.g. $243+405px+...$. Do not accept e.g. $^5C_0 \times 243 \times (px)^0$ for this mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Given that
$\bullet$ $B = 18D$
$\bullet$ $p < 0$
(b) find
(i) the value of $p$
(ii) the value of $C$
(6)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b)(i)
M1: $(B=)5\times3^4p$ $(=405p)$ or $(D=)10\times3^2p^3$ $(=90p^3)$ (simplified or unsimplified including unprocessed indices). The coefficients of B or D may be embedded within the binomial expansion such as $...+5\times3^4px+...+10\times3^2(px)^3$. Also allow e.g. $\binom{5}{1}3^4p$ or $\binom{5}{3}3^2p^3$ or $^5C_13^4p$ or $^5C_33^2p^3$
A1: $(B=)5\times3^4p$ $(=405p)$ and $(D=)10\times3^2p^3$ $(=90p^3)$ (simplified or unsimplified) Allow this mark if the coefficients have not been isolated from x and $x^3$, but the brackets around $(px)$ and $(px)^3$ must be correctly removed. Binomial notation such as $^5C_1$ or $^5C_3$ must have been evaluated.
M1: Uses "B"=18"D" to form a cubic equation in p and attempts to take out a factor of p or divide by p leading to $p^2=...$ (or may be implied by their value of p). "B"="D" is M0. Condone equations involving x and $x^3$ as long as they are removed as they proceed to $p^2=...$. Note that equations may have been simplified before they are formed by cancelling factors e.g. $3^2, 3, 5$ or $p$ so look carefully at equations which are acceptable such as $5\times3^2p=180p^3$ or $9=36p^2 \Rightarrow p^2=...$ (condone if negative). Note $405p=90p^3 \Rightarrow p=\pm\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}$ scores M1A1M0A0 in (b)(i) (did not use "B"=18"D"). They can proceed in (b)(ii) to score M1A0.
A1: $p=-\frac{1}{2}$ only following correct coefficients for B and D (the positive root and $p=0$ must be rejected if found / a clear choice of $p=-\frac{1}{2}$). Can only be scored provided all previous marks have been awarded. Note if the coefficients of B and D are incorrect leading to $p=-\frac{1}{2}$ then this is max M0A0M1A0 in (b) and M1A0 in (c).
Alternative method (b)(i): If the expansion is written as $243(1+5(\frac{px}{3})+\frac{5\times4}{2!}(\frac{px}{3})^2+\frac{5\times4\times3}{3!}(\frac{px}{3})^3)$ then 243 is not required to find p as this will cancel from both sides when setting "B"=18"D".
M1: $(B=)(243\times)5(\frac{p}{3})$ or $(D=)(243\times)\frac{5\times4\times3}{3!}(\frac{p}{3})^3$ (unsimplified with or without the 243)
A1: $(B=)(243\times)5(\frac{p}{3})$ and $(D=)(243\times)\frac{5\times4\times3}{3!}(\frac{p}{3})^3$ (unsimplified either both with or both without the 243 included). Allow this mark if the coefficients have not been isolated from x and $x^3$, but the brackets around $(\frac{px}{3})$ and $(\frac{px}{3})^3$ must be correctly removed.
